content.thinking:
The samples directory is empty, so I'll plan the loft approach using an elliptical sweep profile with rounded sides (around 10) for the fuselage, following a path along the Z-axis with stations running from nose to tail, using the Z-direction as the up vector for the cross-section frame.

I'm sketching out concrete dimensions for the plane now: floor at y=0, wheel radius 0.48, and a series of fuselage stations from the firewall at z=1.95 back to the tail at z=-3.8, each with its own height, width, and vertical offset to give the body a chubby, whimsical taper. I'm also working out the cowl as a lathed profile around the fuselage axis near the nose.

For the cowl itself, I'm simplifying the design: a solid barrel shape with a cream polished front lip, a darker recessed center disk, a ring of nine small brass-grey cylinder heads poking through near the lip, and a brass dome hub at the center to suggest a radial engine.

I'm placing a brass spinner cone at the very front for the propeller, then moving on to figuring out cowl paint details like vent slits and the vertical positioning of the upper and lower wings relative to the fuselage.

Checking clearances: fuselage top sits at 1.98, pilot head top around 2.5, and I'm raising the upper wing to y=2.85 with its bottom at 2.77 to give proper headroom, matching the real Stearman's wing gap. I'm also adding forward stagger to the upper wing and cabane struts connecting it to the fuselage top.

Now I'm working out the front and rear cabane strut positions along z, making sure they don't collide with the cockpits—placing the wing center slightly forward so leading/trailing edges clear the pilot seating, then positioning the front and rear cockpit openings accordingly.

Now I'm positioning the lower wing with less stagger, centered chord around z=0.15, spanning about 7.8 units, and adding a slight dihedral so the tips rise a bit toward the end.

Working out the wing taper profile, tapering the chord width smoothly toward rounded tips with a sweep that narrows near the edges rather than ending abruptly.

I'm thinking about wing paint patterns too — yellow top with red tip accents and rib lines, cream underside, using the normal direction to distinguish top from bottom surfaces. Now I'm figuring out the aileron geometry, extruding a flat plate along the wing's trailing edge using span and chord-backward axes to determine its orientation and thickness direction.

Shaping aileron outline...

I need to mirror the hinge direction for the right wing side so thickness normals stay consistent, then add the four aileron joints since the Stearman has ailerons on both upper and lower wings. For the interplane struts, I'm working out the strut positions along the span, planning front and rear strut pairs on each side for the N-strut configuration.

I'm sketching streamlined strut geometry: thin in the chordwise direction but elongated fore-aft to mimic an airfoil cross-section, figuring out the right orientation for the rod's elliptical radius so it stays narrow sideways while being longer along the strut's fore-aft axis.

Now I'm planning the rigging wires — crossed flying and bracing wires between the struts and wing roots, plus a few connecting the cabane struts to the fuselage, aiming for around sixteen thin rods total before moving on to the landing gear's V-struts.

For the landing gear, I'm positioning paired front and rear struts per side running from the fuselage belly down to an axle, adding a spreader and axle fairing, and sizing the tire as a torus so its bottom sits exactly at y=0. I'm also detailing the wheel hubs with cream caps and red rings over painted spokes.

I'll compute the spoke paint procedurally by finding the polar angle around each wheel's center, writing a reusable wheelPaint function since the two wheels have different centers. Now I'm working out the tail fin's cross-section geometry, deriving the extrusion thickness direction by taking the cross product of the outline's drawing axes to orient it properly along the fuselage.

For the rudder, I'm defining it as a hinged piece with a vertical hinge joint behind the fin, mapping the outline points as back-distance from the hinge versus height. For the horizontal stabilizer, I'm setting up a symmetric span-wise outline similar to how I handled the ailerons.

Now I'm placing the elevators with hinges along the stabilizer's trailing edge, giving them rounded, scalloped tips for a whimsical look, and sizing the stab to about 2.4m total span. I'm also adding small tail struts connecting the fin top to the stabilizer, plus a tail wheel assembly near the rear of the fuselage, accounting for the plane's tail-dragger stance where the fuselage centerline rises slightly toward the tail.

I'm now checking the overall tail height against a real Stearman reference—our fuselage tail sits too high compared to a typical three-point stance, so I'm lowering the tail end and adjusting the stabilizer and tail wheel positions accordingly, along with the leaf-spring strut connecting the tail wheel axle to the fuselage.

Working through fuselage station heights from the cockpit back to the tail, checking belly clearance against the lower wing root and landing gear struts, then confirming prop tip clearance above the ground given the propeller's diameter and mounting height ahead of the cowl. I'm also sketching the rear-seat pilot figure with a rounded torso, leather jacket, and a helmeted head with large round goggles.

For the windscreens, I'm thinking of simple tilted glass plates in brass frames, placing the front cockpit windshield sized around 0.7 wide and 0.3 tall based on where the fuselage top sits.

For the cockpit openings themselves, I'll add dark elliptical recesses into the top deck with a torus coaming rim—padded leather look in cream or tan—positioned where the deck surface meets the centerline.

Instead I'll sweep a closed oval path along a ring to form the hatch rim, rather than trying to cut a plane through the whole fuselage, then drape it onto the deck surface.

For the dark cockpit interior fill, I'll place a thin flattened disc scaled into an ellipse just above the deck, positioned to match the curvature where the deck dips near the fuselage edges.

I'm also planning to raise the pilot seats a bit so the torso emerges naturally over the disc, add tan leather coaming around the cockpit rim, and sketch out side decals — a cream circle emblem with a star and lettering on the fuselage panel.

I'm tempted by whimsical touches like giving the cowl cartoon eyes, Disney Planes-style, but decide that's too risky and settle for a more tasteful, understated decoration instead.

Rather than a face, I'll paint "DAISY MAE" in curly script on the fuselage side, with daisy-flower roundel badges (petals, red/cream/teal) on the upper and lower wings. I'm also considering yellow paint with cream ribs and red wing tips, plus bunting strung between the interplane struts and cabane for a festive finish.

Writing bunting flag geometry...

For the final details, I'm adding exhaust stack pipes at the nose sides, a ring of rivet spheres around the cowl lip, painted panel lines and rivet dots on the fuselage, and a turtledeck headrest fairing behind the pilot shaped as a scaled sphere with cream trim.

I'm also planning a flowing scarf trailing behind the pilot using a swept thin ribbon with cream/red stripes, a pitot tube on a strut, wing struts with small brass cylinder fittings, flat-colored navigation lights (red left, green right) on the wingtips, and maybe a small strapped suitcase on the lower wing for charm, skipping finer control horn details for now.

Deciding where to place the suitcase—settling on strapping it to the lower wing root near the struts with small rope straps rather than the turtledeck, which risks blocking the cockpit view. I'm also considering adding small wedge-shaped wheel chocks under the wheels as a cute ground detail, while skipping extras like a bucket.

For barnstormer flair, I like the idea of a streamlined fuel tank capsule on the upper wing center section in cream with a red stripe, plus a small pennant flagpole with a swallowtail flag streaming off the top wing. I'm also adding anti-slip walkway stripes at the lower wing root.

For joints, I'm planning hinge roles for the propeller, left/right wheels, tail wheel with swivel, rudder, left/right elevators, and four ailerons — keeping it modest at around 14 joints, with the root "body" joint positioned near the cockpit and everything else parented to it. I'll skip extra articulation like the pilot's scarf or dog features since they're not essential, and I'll merge repeated small parts to stay well under the part count limit.

For the texture budget, I'm calculating texel density based on a roughly 150m² painted area, landing on a 2048 atlas for about 0.7cm texel resolution, and deciding to paint only the main surfaces — fuselage, cowl, wings, tail, tires — while leaving struts and rods as flat colors to keep the painted area manageable.

Now I'm defining a cheerful, whimsical color palette: tomato red, cream, sunny yellow for the wings, teal, sky blue glass, leather brown, wood tone, dark accent, brass, steel, tan, pink, and navy for the pilot's jacket.

I'm sketching the whimsical proportions (chubby fuselage, big cowl, stubby wheels) and planning the wing paint scheme — yellow tops with cream rib stripes spaced along the wing, red tip caps, and a stitched cream tape detail near the leading edge.

Working out the rib and tape pattern along the wing surface, adding matching cream ribs on the underside, and considering a red leading-edge band or rounded center stripe near the wing root.

I'm now settling on a bright triad color scheme — red, yellow, and teal — trying out whether the upper wing should have yellow with teal leading-edge bands and tips, or the reverse with red bands, while keeping the lower wing's accents complementary for contrast.

I'm defining the fuselage paint logic: a red base with a scalloped cream belly whose boundary follows a sine wave for a playful wavy edge, plus a thin pinstripe and rivet dot rows, and a teal gradient tip near the tail.

Still defining paint masks...

I'm now planning the cowl region from z 1.95 to 2.55 with the red barrel, teal ring, cream front lip, and five dark gill slits along the sides. Then I need to set up decal surfaces and SVG textures, starting with a daisy-roundel badge for the wings using a circular ring and petal pattern.

For the fuselage I'm sketching a "DAISY MAE" banner decal, considering a tail fin sun/cloud motif or striped rudder design in red, cream, and teal, plus suitcase stickers and triangular flag pennants. I'm also thinking through the goggles as small brass-rimmed cylinders with glass lenses, and sizing the character details like the low-poly head sphere and a hemisphere-based leather helmet.

Now I'm setting up the module imports and builder scaffolding for the biplane, defining a root body joint and small helper functions for creating rods and spheres to construct the character and plane parts.

I'm also designing a merging system that groups geometries by color into buckets, applying transform matrices for position, rotation, and scale, then consolidating each color group into a single merged mesh with flat shading for the final model.

Now I'm defining the fuselage using a loft: a sequence of elliptical cross-section stations positioned along the body, connected with a Catmull-Rom curve through roughly a dozen sides, with rounded caps and appropriate paint color.

For the cowl, I'm lathing a radial profile around the engine axis to create the front nose cowling, shaping it with a tapered lip, a flat recessed front face, and a protruding engine detail with darker and brass-colored accents.

I'm detailing the engine face with cylinder heads arranged radially, using small tapered cylinders to approximate dome shapes, with paint logic distinguishing dark recess versus brass accents by radius and surface normal.

Then I'm building the center hub and spinner cone as a lathed brass dome with a teal tip, followed by the propeller hinge joint and blade extrusion setup.

Working out blade outline coordinates...

Working out the twist for mirrored propeller blades...

I'll skip the pitch idea for now and group the propeller parts under one bone. For the wings, I'm defining a helper function that builds each wing from a path with a dihedral angle and a chord/thickness profile that tapers smoothly toward the tips.

Writing wing geometry logic...

Now I'm figuring out the elliptical cross-section for the wing, with different chord ratios for the upper and lower surfaces, and placing the aileron hinge line at a fraction of the chord so the thickness factor there scales correctly.

I decide to go with slightly whimsical trailing control surfaces that extend a bit beyond the wing's trailing edge, treating the ailerons as separate colored plates with beveled edges and scalloped backs rather than cutting them into the wing planform itself.

I'll extend the plate further back for better visibility, then move on to structural details like the interplane struts, cabane, and wires. For the fuel tank, I'm planning a lofted elliptical capsule on top of the wing center, painted cream with a red stripe and brass cap, and I need to figure out pilot and dog placement using spheres and capsules attached to the body bone, starting with the rear cockpit position.

Now I'm working out the pilot's pose: a capsule torso in a teal jacket, a head with leather helmet and goggles pushed up, rosy cheeks, a grin, and a whimsical handlebar moustache fitting the barnstormer theme, with facial features positioned relative to the forward-facing head and arms reaching toward a control stick near the cockpit.

For the dog, I'm placing a scaled sphere head with a forward snout, dark nose, floppy ears, pushed-up goggles, and a pink tongue, sitting low in the front cockpit with a cream fur body mostly hidden, paws gripping the coaming edge, and a red scarf looping the neck with its tail streaming back along the fuselage, mirroring the pilot's own trailing scarf.

Now I'm working out placement for the fuselage name decal, positioning it on the side surface near the tail section with the correct offset and facing direction, and mirroring it for the opposite side.

Working out the cross product: forward (-1,0,0) × up (0,1,0) gives right = (0,0,-1), meaning on the left side the viewer's right points toward -z, the tail direction, so the text would read from front to back.

Checking the right side similarly: there the viewer's right points toward +z, meaning text there reads tail-to-nose, matching the standard convention of nose facing right on that side — no mirroring needed, text stays legible on both sides.

For the font, I'll fall back to a serif stack like Georgia, Times New Roman, serif with bold italic styling in case Georgia isn't available in headless Chrome. Now I need to figure out the decal dimensions.

I'm placing wing badge decals on the upper and lower wing surfaces using ellipsoid-friendly orientation vectors, then working out bunting strings that hang between the wingtip fittings, the front interplane struts, and the cabane, planning to sample points along each path with some sag for a natural drape.

Now I'm sizing the wheel assembly: a torus tire with hub and rim radii totaling 0.5, a cylindrical hub disc with painted spoke details based on radial angle from center, and considering a cream fairing cover over the wheel.

For the hubcaps, I'm going with whimsical oversized domes using a lathe profile with a shallow curved outline, painted in a red/cream pinwheel pattern.

For the inner hub, the plain disc sits flush while the outer side has a small dome; the wheel joint hinges at the axle with the bone aligned outward along x, and I'm keeping the structure simple—tire torus plus disc for each side, mirrored for symmetry.

Now I'm working out the single-lathe solution: a symmetric profile mirrored in y lets one lathe form both hub faces at once, painted red/cream in wedges, sized to fit within the tire width while letting the hubcap domes protrude slightly. Then I'm figuring out the gear strut geometry, running V-shaped struts from the fuselage belly down to the axle ends for both front and rear legs.

I'm placing the wheel joints and axle positions, adding a streamlined cream fairing sleeve over the axle rod where it passes under the fuselage belly, and sketching the tail wheel setup with a curved leaf-spring strut leading to a small tire torus. Now I'm starting to work out the horizontal stabilizer's vertical position based on the tail station dimensions.

Shifting to the vertical fin, I'm defining its base extent along the fuselage and its height, then sketching outline coordinates for the fin shape — plotting points that sweep from the leading edge base up to the top, splitting the fin into a fixed front section and a hinged rudder section near the back.

Now I'm setting up the rudder as a separate extrusion joined at a hinge point further back, giving it a rounded, slightly whimsical top profile. For paint, I'm thinking of applying vertical striped bands in red, cream, and teal across the fin and rudder surfaces, using a modulo pattern on the x-coordinate to cycle through the three colors.

Deciding to keep the fin simple, matching the fuselage red with a teal tip rather than adding a decal. I'm moving on to the horizontal stabilizer and elevators, defining them as a spanwise extrusion with a fixed stabilizer section and separate elevator sections further aft, and working out the outline points for the front and back edges of the span.

Writing elevator outline coordinates...

Checking the stabilizer plate extends properly past the fuselage tail without clipping, and verifying the fin top position and brace strut connections between fin and stabilizer stay within reasonable proportions.

Now I'm working out where the cabane struts attach to the fuselage top versus the wing, computing the fuselage surface height at the strut base x-position using the ellipse cross-section formula, then figuring out where that connects up to the top wing's leading edge.

Checking that the front strut at z=.95 falls within the upper wing's chord span, and setting the rear struts to run vertically from (±2.5,1.18,-0.2) to (±2.5,2.8,0.1), keeping them parallel and un-tilted in x for that classic Stearman look.

Now I'm thinking through the rigging wires: adding X-pattern cross wires within the strut bay between the front and rear struts, plus flying wires running from the strut tops down to the fuselage, making sure they pass just above the lower wing surface rather than through it.

Since the lower wing's outer section is cantilevered out to 3.9m while the upper tip extends to 4.3, I'm considering adding an extra outer strut around x=3.6 to help brace that span, slanting it between the lower wing and the structure above.

I'm settling on one bay of struts per side (around x=1.7 and 3.5) with wire bracing at the tips, similar to a Stearman layout. The upper wing's center section passes continuously over the fuselage, while the lower wing simply passes through the body where it intersects at y=1.12, which should be fine geometrically. I'm also thinking about adding dark non-slip walkway paint strips on the lower wing's upper surface near the wing roots as a detail.

Now I'm adding small details: nav lights (red and green spheres) at the wingtips, a pitot tube off the front strut, a brass compass drum on the cabane, and maybe a whimsical tiny lantern hung on the front strut. I'm also working out exhaust pipes curving back from the cowl sides using bezier sweeps with a flared brass ring at the end, and considering whether to add a wingtip skid bow before moving on to the wing leading edge.

Then I'm deciding against a turtledeck bulge in favor of a simple brown capsule headrest pad behind the pilot, skipping smoke puffs and cockpit cords, adding small dark oval footholds on the fuselage side, and designing a fluttering scarf as a bezier ribbon trailing from the pilot's neck, working out the orientation so it reads as a thin flat ribbon rather than a vertical strip.

I'm sketching the scarf's wavy catmull-rom path with sinusoidal offsets, applying alternating pink and cream paint bands along its length, and confirming it'll trail cleanly above the fuselage without clipping the tail. I'm also considering adding a painted name on the nose, then tallying up the remaining parts needed—cowl rivets, engine cylinders, strut fittings, wheel bolts—before starting to write the actual construction code using the part and rod API.

Now I'm working through the geometry helpers available: rod and capsule take color right after radius, sweep can follow a path with variable radius and optional color argument, and there are also extrude, lathe, decal, cards, and surface functions for different shape types. I'm defining a reusable strut helper for the wing struts, debating whether rod's radius parameter can accept a function for tapering, and deciding to fall back to sweep directly with an explicit radius function and flat caps to be safe when building two-point paths.

For the wire/strut geometry I'm confirming sweep accepts a plain point array as a polyline and checking whether rod supports a sides option for polygon cross-sections. For color accents, I'm picking dark plum tires with cream hubs instead of plain black for a more whimsical look. Now I'm laying out the fuselage cross-section stations with z positions and corresponding center y, width, and height values to interpolate the body profile, then sizing the engine cowl intentionally larger than the fuselage radius at the nose to give it a chubby, whimsical look.

Writing paint shader logic...

Adding more panel line seams...

Still defining wing shape logic...

I'm defining color constants as strings, then working out aileron paint stripes alternating cream and trim colors along the span, plus wheel details. Now I'm starting to write the actual file, setting up a helper map and matrix/quaternion utilities for placing merged geometry bits.

Still writing placement helpers...

I'm adding an orientation helper that aligns a cylinder's axis to a given direction using a quaternion, then a bitDir function that applies position and direction together. Finally I'm sketching the flush step that merges each color group's geometries and attaches them as parts to the appropriate bones.

I'm now setting up bins keyed by bone and color combinations so wheel bits stay separated, planning the file's imports from the builder, frame, math, path, paint, and texture modules, and drafting the metadata block with name, description, style, and commit info.

Defining the color palette...

Now I'm setting up the builder structure, creating the body joint and hinge points for the propeller and other moving parts.

Defining joint hinges and aileron geometry...

Adjusting the outline slightly with a small negative overlap into the wing, then extruding with thickness and bevel. For the hinge joint I'm placing it at the outer x position along the back offset, and reconsidering the lower wing aileron dimensions with a shorter span and length.

I'm writing a wing-generation function that builds a path from wingtip through center to the other tip with dihedral offset, using a polyline instead of a smooth curve so dihedral kinks stay sharp while sweep corners get rounded. I'm also defining a radius function along the path and setting sweep options like color, bone, sides, and caps for rendering the wing shape.

Now I'm moving on to the pilot figure, placing the rear cockpit seat position and building the torso as a capsule, then adding a brown leather jacket with a cream sheepskin collar as a closed ring sweep around the neck, and finally a skin-toned sphere for the head positioned above the torso.

I'm shaping the flight cap as a partial sphere geometry tilted back with cream ear flaps, then adding goggles pushed up on the forehead using small cylinders for lenses with brass rim torus shapes and a strap swept as a closed circle around the head.

For the face, I'm placing a small pink nose sphere, curling capsule shapes for an orange moustache, a dark mouth sweep, and pink cheek discs. I'm making the eyes read as cute googly eyes inside the goggle lenses—white flattened spheres with dark pupils and glints, rimmed in brass—rather than drawing separate eyes that would be hidden. Now I'm setting up shoulder points and arm capsules reaching down toward the hands.

Continuing down the arms, I'm adding teal forearm capsules, brown glove spheres for hands, and a steel control stick with a red knob rising between them. Then I'm shifting to the dog character riding in the front cockpit—positioning its head and body spheres with brown fur and a cream muzzle patch, adding a snout capsule, a dark nose sphere, and floppy ear capsules in a darker brown.

Now I'm equipping the dog with goggles (small eye lenses), a tiny pink tongue, and paw spheres resting on the cockpit coaming. I'm also sketching a red scarf sweeping back from its neck, checking it clears the cabane struts, and starting to lay out the front windscreen shape as an extruded outline tilted to match the fuselage line.

Adding a dark flattened cylinder inside the coaming ring to suggest an empty cockpit interior, scaling it to fit within the draped ring's oval shape.

Now I'm placing brass rivets around the cowl lip radius for detail, and seam rivets along the rear cowl band, before positioning the fuel tank capsule centered on top of the upper wing surface.

I'll add small flagpoles with swallow-tailed pennants at both wingtips (x≈±4.15), with nav lights below them, bringing the total height to roughly 3.4 m.

I'm also considering stringing a sagging bunting banner across the top—from the left wingtip pole over the tank cap to the right wingtip pole—to give a festive swagged-flag look visible from the front.

Poles get brass finials and a small streaming swallow-tail pennant in teal/red. For the cards, I'll orient their frames to face upward and keep textures muted grey-white with a thin stitched border, letting the pennant/card colors carry the palette.

Now I'm adding a suitcase prop on the lower wing — tan box with brass corners, red straps, a handle, and sticker decals on top via a plane decal. I'm sketching extra details like luggage straps and a wing-walker rail but deciding to skip those, then considering wheel chocks as a small triangular wedge prism placed behind the wheels.

Working out the chock placement geometry...

Skipping the rope detail, I'll decide cowl paint shading based on radial distance from the engine's axis center, then move to finalizing the code with proper typed arrays.

I'm setting up a wire helper for rods using thin steel cylinders, strut sweeps with octagonal cross-sections, and small brass fitting cylinders at strut ends, then planning to write the full function in one pass before checking it against a preview. I'm also sketching an SVG texture for hanging pennant cards with a defined viewBox and bottom edge geometry.

For the flipped pennant drawing, I'm working out that the root edge (bottom of the SVG) ends up at the top once flipped upside down, so the triangle needs its wide base near the bottom of the drawing coordinates and its apex near the top, which after flipping places the base correctly at the top on screen like a real bunting flag.

Now I'm sketching a daisy badge SVG: an outer circle with cream fill and red stroke, a ring of petal ellipses arranged radially around the center using rotation transforms, and a smaller yellow center circle outlined in red, making sure there are at least a few petals for a convincing flower shape.

For the ribbon-style name banner, I'm sizing it generously (bumping to 512px) since smaller text like a subtitle would become unreadable at decal resolution, so I'll drop the subtitle and keep just the bold italic red name with a small flower accent. Then I'm planning a simple suitcase sticker with stars-and-stripes styling at a compact 100x70 viewBox.

Now I'm positioning decals on the plane: a roundel on the upper wingtip, and a badge on both sides of the tail fin, calculating the local coordinates and facing directions needed for each decal placement so they land correctly on the fin's thin extruded surface. With placements worked out, I'm ready to write the actual file.

input.command: mkdir -p scratch/barnstormerBiplane; grep -n "export" src/frame.ts | head -20; grep -n "export type SweepOptions" -A60 src/sweep.ts | head -90
